UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE  
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
)
Docket No. ER26-3515-000
 
COMMENTS AND LIMITED PROTEST OF THE NRG COMPANIES 
 
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”) 
Rules of Practice and Procedures,1 the NRG Companies2 (“NRG”) respectfully submit these 
comments and limited protest in response to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) August 13, 
2026, filing proposing to establish interim resource adequacy service (“IRAS”) and a large load 
registry to address system reliability (“PJM IRAS Filing” or “IRAS Filing”). 
In general, NRG supports PJM’s efforts to provide certainty and clarity to market 
participants and New Large Loads3 that do not bring new supply into the PJM market. NRG also 
supports PJM’s efforts to articulate rules pertaining to the curtailment of New Large Loads that 
 
1 18 C.F.R. § 385.211 (2026).  
2 The NRG Companies include the following subsidiaries of NRG Energy, Inc. (“NRG”): 
NRG Business Marketing LLC, Aspen Gen Funding, LLC, Direct Energy Business, LLC, 
Doswell, LLC, Energy Plus Holdings LLC, Enerwise Global Technologies, LLC d/b/a CPower, 
Green Mountain Energy Company, Helix Ironwood, LLC, Independence Energy Group LLC, 
LSP University Park, LLC, Midwest Generation LLC, NRG Curtailment Solutions, Inc., Reliant 
Energy Northeast LLC, Riverside Generating Company, LLC, Stream Energy Pennsylvania, 
LLC, University Park Energy, LLC and XOOM Energy, LLC. The NRG Companies have 
separately moved to intervene in this proceeding. See (doc-less) Motion to Intervene of NRG 
Business Marketing LLC, et al., Docket No. ER26-3515-000 (filed Aug. 31, 2026). 
3 Terms utilized herein that are not otherwise defined have the meaning ascribed by the 
PJM IRAS Filing’s proposed definitions or the PJM Tariff.

2 
do not bring new supply where such customers are curtailed before existing pre-emergency and 
emergency customers. 
However, PJM’s proposal contains elements that are unjust, unreasonable, unduly 
discriminatory, and must be revised. These consist of (i) PJM’s permanent exclusion of every 
Demand Resource4 that has ever supported a capacity commitment in any prior Delivery Year 
and (ii) the requirement for new capacity serving New Large Loads to bid into the capacity 
market as a price-taker for 10 years without certain necessary protections for asset owners. 
Finally, there are a number of clarifications NRG seeks related to the IRAS requirements around 
Demand Resources.  
 
I. 
ABOUT NRG 
Through various subsidiaries, NRG owns or controls over 9 GW of generation in PJM as 
well as generation in adjacent markets that can be imported into the PJM market. Additionally, 
NRG subsidiaries provide retail power throughout PJM and two NRG subsidiaries provide 
Demand Resources in PJM. Thus, NRG actively participates in the organized markets 
administered by PJM, including the PJM capacity market.  
 
II. 
BACKGROUND 
The PJM IRAS Filing creates a new supplemental capacity product through which New 
Large Loads may provide a load reduction service during periods of insufficient capacity instead 
 
4 This limited protest refers to Demand Resources and Distributed Energy Resources 
(“DER”) Capacity Aggregation Resources, as the terms are defined by the PJM OATT, as 
“Demand Resources” to improve readability, but is not intended to refer only to Demand 
Resources with the term unless the context requires otherwise.

3 
of participating in the Base Residual Auction (“BRA”). IRAS resources will be issued 
curtailment instructions prior to PJM calling on Pre-Emergency Load Management. For 
providing the reduction, PJM proposes an IRAS rate equal to 50% of the Non-Performance 
Charge Rate, with flexibility for Electric Distributors and states to reduce the rate or for eligible 
New Large Loads to waive compensation entirely.  
Instead of participating as an IRAS resource, New Large Loads may instead meet their 
capacity obligations through a Bring Your Own New Capacity (“BYONC”) option. BYONC is 
defined as megawatts of new Unforced Capacity (“UCAP”) that meet the eligibility criteria set 
forth in Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section VI.5 A single physical resource may support multiple 
BYONC arrangements with different New Large Loads, and a New Large Load may enter into 
BYONC arrangements with discrete resources.6 BYONC must be supported by: (1) a new-build 
generation resource (including resources obtaining Capacity Interconnection Rights transferred 
from deactivated resources); (2) incremental capacity from an uprate; (3) incremental capacity 
from Surplus Interconnection Service; (4) repowering of a deactivated resource that deactivated 
prior to April 10, 2026; or (5) incremental capacity from a fuel-type change.7 BYONC may also 
be supported by Planned Demand Resources or Planned DER Capacity Aggregation 
Resources. However, PJM has proposed to only permit BYONC to be supported by Demand 
Resources if those resources “did not previously support a capacity commitment or reduce the 
amount of capacity needed to meet the PJM Reliability Requirement … for or prior to the 
 
5 Proposed Tariff, Definitions (“Bring Your Own New Capacity”).  
6 Proposed Tariff, Attach. DD-4, section VII(f). 
7 Proposed Tariff, Attach. DD-4, section VI(b)(i).

4 
2026/27 Delivery Year” 8 – thus permanently excluding every Demand Resource that has ever 
supported a capacity commitment in any prior Delivery Year.  
Each BYONC must participate as a price taker ($0/MW offer) in BRAs for 10 
consecutive Delivery Years, starting with the first Delivery Year of the arrangement. BYONC is 
also subject to the capacity must-offer requirement and is prohibited from seeking an exception 
to provide an external sale during the 10-year period. BYONC supported by a Demand Resource 
or DER Capacity Aggregation Resource also has a 10-year commitment, but the seller may 
replace its BYONC obligation with a different qualifying resource, subject to conditions. This 
provides a “bridge to power” allowing near-term demand-supported capacity to be eventually 
replaced with new generation. Additionally, beginning with the 2029/30 Delivery Year, PJM 
proposes to exclude from the VRR Curve the MW of New Large Loads that have not entered 
into BYONC arrangements and do not have allocated capacity (IRAS resources), above and 
beyond the MW included in the 2028/29 Delivery Year load forecast.  
BYONC BRA participation requirements (including the price-taker obligation) are 
extinguished if IRAS is not needed for three consecutive Delivery Years. At that point, BYONC 
resources become regular Capacity Resources, though still subject to the general capacity must-
offer requirement. If the PJM Region meets its reliability requirements for three consecutive 
Delivery Years and then re-enters shortage, the “new” benchmark resets. Demand-side capacity 
would then be measured against registration “in the Delivery Year prior to the first Delivery 
Year” in which PJM is again short of capacity. 
 
8 Proposed Tariff, Attach. DD-4, section VI(b)(ii).

5 
III. 
COMMENTS IN SUPPORT OF THE PJM IRAS FILING 
In general, NRG supports PJM’s IRAS Filing. PJM proposes to require Load Serving 
Entities (“LSEs”) to “bring new capacity in an amount that equals or exceeds its New Large 
Loads’ peak load or be subject to load reduction requests during Emergencies prior to Pre-
Emergency Load Management Response.”9 PJM notes that it is “currently short of capacity and 
looking to reestablish healthy capacity reserve margin.”10 PJM’s approach is commonsense: New 
Large Loads must be supported by Capacity Resources. Furthermore, NRG supports the 
requirement that the BYONC capacity be “new” generation.  
NRG also supports PJM’s proposal to curtail New Large Loads before existing 
customers, including Pre-Emergency and Emergency Demand Response customers. Specifically, 
the PJM IRAS Filing provides that “PJM can call on IRAS load reductions prior to calling on 
Pre-Emergency Load Management Reductions Actions when needed to avoid a capacity 
shortage.”11 As PJM notes, this provision does not identify the specific load that an Electric 
Distributor must reduce.12 Rather, the Electric Distributor, in coordination with the appropriate 
states and/or Relevant Electric Retail Regulatory Authorities, LSEs, and LSE customers, will 
determine which loads should ultimately be curtailed.13 The proposed curtailment obligation 
 
9 PJM IRAS Filing at 3-4, 49.  
10 Id. at 52.  
11 PJM IRAS Filing at 25 (citing Proposed Tariff, Attach. DD-4, Section 1(b)).  
12 PJM IRAS Filing at 26.  
13 Id. Nonetheless, PJM should consider clarifying that if Electric Distributors, in 
coordination with these entities, do not take action, PJM will use the registry to curtail New 
Large Loads ahead of all other loads.

6 
gives states and LSEs latitude to curtail efficiently and, in particular, to prioritize customers that 
curtail voluntarily. The construct also provides a “bridge to power” that protects existing 
customers.  
 
IV. 
LIMITED PROTEST 
Pursuant to the Commission’s Rule 211,14 NRG provides the following limited protest. 
As written, the tariff proposed by PJM fails to be just and reasonable and is unduly 
discriminatory because it (i) excludes otherwise capable Demand Resources based on an 
unwarranted permanent bar to such resources that have participated in any prior BRA; and 
(ii) imposes an overly broad and unjust and unreasonable ten-year price-taker obligation on all 
BYONC resources. 
PJM has consented to the Commission’s exercise of authority to modify or sever any 
element of the filing to the extent necessary, so long as the modification is consistent with PJM’s 
overarching objectives.15 Thus, the Commission has authority to modify PJM’s proposed tariff in 
the manner proposed by NRG by directing a compliance filing.16 NRG’s modest proposals do not 
 
14 18 C.F.R. § 385.211. 
15 PJM IRAS Filing at 9 (citing NRG Power Marketing LLC v. FERC, 862 F.3d 108 (D.C. 
Cir. 2017)). 
16 N.Y. Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 188 FERC ¶ 61,051, at P 22 n.36 (2024) (citing NRG 
Power Mktg., LLC v. FERC, 862 F.3d 108, 114-15 (D.C. Cir. 2017)) (“the Commission has 
‘authority to propose modifications to a utility’s [FPA section 205] proposal if the utility consents 
to the modifications.’ ”).

7 
conflict with PJM’s Board Directive, or with the objectives reflected in the Critical Issue Fast 
Path’s (“CIFP”) accelerated stakeholder process related to the PJM IRAS Filing.17 
A. New Demand Resources Should Be Permitted to Bid into the Market to Support 
New Large Loads Regardless of Prior Market Participation 
PJM states that new capacity, BYONC, is at a basic level, “megawatts of Unforced 
Capacity” and thus is “consistent with how Capacity Resources under PJM’s capacity market 
design are also MW and not the underlying physical resource.”18 PJM explains that BYONC is 
“designed to offset the capacity need presented by the New Large Load.”19 PJM further explains 
that “new capacity may be supported by generation, storage, or demand-side resources that meet 
certain gating criteria.”20 
However, PJM’s “gating criteria” for BYONC applicable to Demand Resources include a 
requirement that Planned Demand Resources “did not previously support a capacity commitment 
or reduce the amount of capacity needed to meet the PJM Region Reliability Requirement … for 
or prior to the 2026/2027 Delivery Year.”21 This means that PJM has permanently excluded 
every Demand Resource that has ever supported a capacity commitment in any prior Delivery 
 
17 See PJM IRAS Filing at 17-18 (citing Letter from Paula Conboy, Chair, PJM Board of 
Managers, Board Decisional Letter on Critical Issue Fast Path – Reliability Backstop 
Procurement and Connect and Manage, 1 (July 27, 2026), https://www.pjm.com/-
/media/DotCom/about-pjm/who-we-are/public-disclosures/2026/20260727-board- 
decisional-letter-on-cifp-reliability-backstop-procurement-and-connect-and-manage.pdf (“PJM 
Board Directive”).  
18 PJM IRAS Filing at 51.  
19 Id.  
20 Id. at 53.  
21 PJM IRAS Filing at 54 (emphasis supplied) (citing Proposed Tariff, Attach. DD-4, 
Sections VI(b)(i)(1)-(5)).

8 
Year even though Demand Resources have proven their value in PJM. They have been critical in 
mitigating emergencies and have helped to “avoid the cost of dispatching [or building] additional 
generation or involuntarily curtailing load.”22 In 2025 alone, PJM successfully relied on Demand 
Resources that provided more than 4,000 MW of capacity during emergencies.23  
Under PJM’s proposal, a customer location that participated as a Demand Resource as far 
back as 200624 and later ceased participation would be ineligible to participate as a BYONC 
capacity resource. The ban on eligibility applies even if the ownership or occupancy at the 
customer location has changed or if there are new flexibility capabilities. For example, a 
customer location that ceased participation as a Demand Resource in 2010 and was no longer in 
any way considered an existing capacity resource would be banned from participation in 
BYONC. This exclusion is patently unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory.25 
First, this restriction applies only to Demand Resources, not to retired generators or 
storage resources that exited the market but could reactivate their Capacity Interconnection 
Rights.26 Deactivated generators also may be “repower[ed]” if they were deactivated before April 
 
22 Fed. Energy Reg. Comm’n, 2025 Assessment of Demand Response and Advanced 
Metering, 16 (Dec. 2025) https://www.ferc.gov/news-events/news/ferc-staff-issues-2025-
assessment-demand-response-and-advanced-metering.  
23 Id. at 17.  
24 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 115 FERC ¶ 61,079, at P 84 (2006). 
25 Xcel Energy Servs. Inc. v. FERC, 41 F.4th 548, 559 (D.C. Cir. 2022) (explaining 
discriminatory standards and referencing the Commission policy that “the Commission can 
promote market entry by ensuring that all generators compete on a level playing field”).  
26 IRAS Filing at 53-54 (citing Proposed Tariff, Attach. DD-4, Sections VI(b)(i)(1)-(5)).

9 
10, 2026 and be considered “new” capacity that can qualify as BYONC.27 PJM has provided no 
explanation or support for allowing deactivated generation that had once participated in a prior 
BRA to participate as BYONC, while excluding Demand Resources that also had participated in 
a prior BRA from qualifying as BYONC.28 The fact that “new” Demand Resources can qualify 
for BYONC just like new generation necessarily means that the nature of the Capacity Resource 
is not a relevant factor to discriminate or differentiate for inclusion as BYONC.29 Therefore, this 
inconsistent treatment of retired generation and Demand Resources that had participated in prior 
BRAs is de facto unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory. 
Second, there is no justification for such discriminatory treatment.30 The discriminatory 
treatment of previously enrolled Demand Resource locations excludes gigawatts of potential 
Demand Resources from qualifying as BYONC. As noted, generation that has deactivated can 
 
27 Id.  
28 West Deptford Energy, LLC v. FERC, 766 F.3d 10, 20-22 (D.C. Cir. 2014) (“the 
Commission would have to provide a reasoned analysis, resting on articulated objective, 
nondiscriminatory, and evenhanded criteria, that would justify treating [one generator] 
differently than the generators in all those other cases.”); FERC v. Elec. Power Supply Ass’n, 577 
U.S. 260, 292 (2016), as revised (Jan. 28, 2016) (noting FERC’s position that demand response 
and other generators should be treated equally because “both provide the same value to a 
wholesale market”).  
29 Tenaska Clear Creek Wind, LLC v. FERC, 108 F.4th 858, 868 (D.C. Cir. 2024) (citation 
omitted) (“[U]ndue discrimination occurs when similarly situated entities are charged different 
rates for no good reason.”); Black Oak Energy, LLC v. FERC, 725 F.3d 230, 239 (D.C. Cir. 2013) 
(allowing FERC to rely upon “differences between parties that are relevant to the achievement of 
permissible policy goals”). 
30 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 115 FERC ¶ 61,079, at P 72-73 (2006) (“We encourage 
PJM to examine and incorporate reasonable accommodations to maximize demand response 
participation in the capacity market.”); 16 U.S.C. § 824d; Wisconsin Pub. Power, Inc. v. FERC, 
493 F.3d 239, 246 (D.C. Cir. 2007) (“Section 205 … prohibits undue discrimination in rates, 
charges, or terms of service.”).

10 
repower or obtain new interconnection rights and participate as BYONC. By contrast, a Demand 
Resource that once participated in a BRA as a Capacity Resource does not need to be repowered 
or obtain new interconnection rights to participate. Allowing such Demand Resources to qualify 
as BYONC can add meaningful capacity immediately by improving the utilization of existing 
resources,31 while aiding PJM in reestablishing the “healthy capacity reserve margins” it seeks 
through the IRAS Filing.32 Moreover, unlike generators or storage resources, Demand Resources 
can grow or shrink in response to price signals. That flexibility is a feature, not a flaw; when 
power prices are high due to demand, Demand Resources can offer greater participation.33 And 
unlike physical generation facilities, Demand Resources can respond with little delay to changes 
in demand signals.34  
Third, allowing Demand Resources that have ceased participation in BRAs in prior 
Delivery Years to qualify as BYONC is consistent with limiting BYONC eligibility for 
generation to new resources. Existing generation resources in PJM are required to offer their 
available unforced capacity into the capacity market. Therefore, existing generation in PJM 
already participates in the BRA and should not be allowed to withdraw from the capacity market 
in order to qualify as BYONC as discussed herein. Demand Resources voluntarily participate in 
the capacity market. Thus, Demand Resources that have participated in past Delivery Years, but 
 
31 New York Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 147 FERC ¶ 61,152, at P 20 (2014) (noting 
resources “such as demand response and repowering options” provide “shorter term capacity 
responses” to meet capacity needs). 
32 PJM IRAS Filing at 52. 
33 Dept. of Energy, Benefits of Demand Response in Electricity Markets and 
Recommendations for Achieving Them, at 13-15 (Feb. 2006).  
34 Id.

11 
ceased participation as Capacity Resources prior to 2026/27, should be allowed to qualify as 
BYONC, as allowing such participation has no negative implications on future BRAs. 
Taken together, these factors contradict how PJM proposes treating these resources. 
Indeed, the flexible and voluntary nature of Demand Resource participation in the PJM capacity 
market supports inclusion of Demand Resources as BYONC, as Demand Resources can provide 
significant immediate capacity to help serve New Large Load rather than relying on IRAS.  
NRG further notes that PJM’s IRAS Filing is inconsistent with the proposal approved by 
the PJM Board. PJM’s July 31, 2026, version of the IRAS proposal – the final public version 
before the PJM IRAS Filing that was approved by the PJM Board – would only restrict Demand 
Resources that had participated in the 2026/27 or 2027/28 Delivery Year.35 This three-year 
limited lookback is just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory because it treats all Capacity 
Resources equally.36 As proposed, the PJM Board has not reviewed the issue herein to deem it 
non-discriminatory.37 However, in the IRAS Filing, PJM bars participation by Demand 
 
35 PJM, PJM Interim Resource Adequacy Service Detailed Proposal, at 7 (July 31, 2026) 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/cifp-rbp/2026/20260731/20260731-
item-02b---cifp-framework-for-service-during-periods-of-insufficient-resource-adequacy---
executive-summary---redline.pdf.  
36 Alabama Elec. Co-op., Inc. v. FERC, 684 F.2d 20, 29 (D.C. Cir. 1982) (“In the typical 
case, where the section 205(b) challenge is raised against a rate design calling for different rates 
to customer classes which are similarly situated.”); New York Pub. Serv. Comm’n v. New York 
Indep. Sys. Op., Inc., 153 FERC ¶ 61,022, at P 79 (2015) (finding a narrowly tailored exemption 
was appropriate).  
37 PJM Operating Agreement § 7.7(vii) (requiring the PJM Board to “review for 
consistency with the creation and operation of a robust, competitive and non-discriminatory 
electric power market in the PJM Region any change to rate design or to non-rate terms and 
conditions proposed by Transmission Owners for filing under section 205 of the Federal 
Power Act”).

12 
Resources that had ever been Capacity Resources in any prior BRA, without explaining the 
departure from the proposal submitted to the Board.  
The IRAS Filing contemplates that, if the PJM Region meets its reliability requirements 
for three consecutive Delivery Years and then re-enters shortage, the “new” benchmark resets. At 
that point, the demand-side gating criterion measures against registration “in the Delivery Year 
prior to the first Delivery Year” in which the PJM Region is short of capacity.38 Here, PJM itself 
recognizes a lookback-window approach is workable and reasonable. There is no principled 
justification for the asymmetry of applying a lookback in one context but not in the related 
Demand Resources context. To address this unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory 
treatment, NRG requests that the Commission adopt a three-year lookback window rather than a 
permanent exclusion.39 Namely, PJM should permit Demand Resources that have not 
participated in the three most recent BRAs to qualify for BYONC.  
The overly broad ineligibility is inconsistent with the policy announced by the Secretary 
of Energy to leverage available backup generation to address the United States’ reliability 
challenges and other grid challenges.40 There are gigawatts of backup generation that were once 
eligible and did participate in demand response but subsequently discontinued participation. 
Demand response participation by backup generators may become economically viable through 
 
38 PJM IRAS Filing at 55 (citing Proposed Tariff, Attach. DD-4, Section VI(b)(ii)(1)). 
39 Id.  
40 Letter from Sec. of Energy Christopher Wright to Reliability Coordinators, Leveraging 
Backup Generation Facilities During Energy Emergencies (Jan. 22, 2026) 
https://www.energy.gov/documents/leveraging-backup-generation-facilities-during-energy-
emergencies (suggesting reliability coordinators “deliberately prioritize the dispatch order of 
backup generation to achieve the greatest benefit to the bulk power system while balancing 
mission-essential functions”).

13 
BYONC arrangements and should be considered as new resources. The BYONC mechanism 
would present a powerful means to leverage this latent backup generation capacity to meet 
today’s reliability challenges and foster economic growth. PJM’s ban on prior customer location 
eligibility to participate in BYONC undermines the Secretary of Energy’s directive to develop 
and encourage backup generation resources. 
In short, a Demand Resource that chooses to re-enter the market still provides new 
capacity to the system, just as a generator that undertakes an uprate project adds new capacity. To 
arbitrarily exclude a Demand Resource from participating solely because it had participated in 
past BRAs, while simultaneously permitting reactivated or repowered generators to qualify, is 
unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory.41 
B. Capacity Serving New Large Loads Should Not Be Required to Bid into the BRA as 
a Price Taker for 10 Years Without a Replacement Mechanism 
PJM proposes that “BYONC must participate, as a price taker (i.e. $0/MW offer) in RPM 
Auctions for 10 consecutive Delivery Years.”42 PJM states that the BYONC arrangement “serves 
as the commitment to provide [] capacity.”43 PJM further states that because the “resource is 
already obligated to provide the capacity, its incremental, going-forward avoidable costs to 
secure the RPM commitment are zero.”44 The ten-year price-taker obligation is not just and 
reasonable as applied to all Capacity Resources, including generation, storage, and demand-side 
resources. NRG’s protest on this point is not limited to Demand Resources. NRG requests that 
 
41 See n.29, supra.  
42 PJM IRAS Filing at 55-56. 
43 Id. at 57.  
44 Id. at 58-59.

14 
the Commission direct PJM to provide opportunities to reflect costs in offers for unknown and/or 
unknowable costs imposed upon the Capacity Resource owner and not otherwise recoverable 
under the terms of the asset owner’s bilateral contracts with large loads. 
A ten-year capacity obligation for a resource is significant.45 Participation as an existing 
Capacity Resource in PJM is subject to a must-offer requirement for capacity auctions only three 
years into the future.46 A ten-year must-offer commitment with a mandatory zero-dollar offer 
compounds the significance of the commitment.47 Circumstances may change materially during a 
ten-year bilateral agreement between third parties, potentially altering a facility’s operating costs 
in unpredictable ways. For instance, new environmental obligations may arise that require capital 
expenditures, a facility may suffer a catastrophic loss, or fuel may become prohibitively 
expensive in a constrained region. Given the corresponding requirement to offer into the BRA at 
zero-cost for 10 years, a BYONC resource cannot be economically replaced as operating and 
market conditions evolve. As a result, this market construct is effectively designed to keep

time, BRAs will have occurred through 2037/38. In this plausible scenario, a BYONC resource 
would be required to offer as a price taker well past when PJM demonstrates sufficient capacity 
to meet all load.   
46 PJM Capacity Manual 18 § 5.7 (rev. 62, Dec. 17, 2025).  
47 The Commission has previously found that even a five-year must-offer obligation may 
be unjust and unreasonable because it ultimately undercompensated sellers. See, e.g., California

finding that a must-offer obligation lasting five years to be unjust and unreasonable and 
undercompensated sellers), vacating on other grounds, City of Anaheim, Cal. v. FERC, 558 F.3d 
521, 526 (D.C. Cir. 2009).

15 
economically inefficient generators operating, potentially at a loss, rather than allowing more 
efficient resources to displace them. 
The Commission should direct PJM to include the opportunity for such costs to be 
reflected in subsequent capacity auctions should conditions such as those described above arise. 
The PJM Tariff already has mechanisms for other resources to reflect their costs through unit 
specific Avoidable Cost Rate (“ACR”) offers.48 NRG proposes a similar approach here. This 
would ensure in the limited cases where otherwise unforeseen circumstances are unaddressed or 
are at issue in bilateral transactions, the resource owner has an opportunity (but not the 
guarantee) to recover such unforeseen costs.49 The ACR approach also offers benefits to PJM 
customers: (1) the market receives the benefit of the zero-offer price for ten years in most cases, 
absent detailed showings; (2) in extraordinary circumstances, the Capacity Resource serving a 
New Large Load is able to continue doing so while recovering exceptional and unforeseen costs; 
(3) more economic resources are able to enter the market and replace highly inefficient Capacity 
Resources; and (4) reliability is improved over the course of the IRAS-imposed commitments.50   
Additionally, to the extent PJM imposes a price-taker requirement on BYONC resources, 
the requirement should not apply to excess capacity beyond the BYONC commitment. If a 
1,200-MW generation facility has committed 700 MW as BYONC, the remaining 500 MW

and documentation” shall be submitted to the IMM for consideration. 
49 If these costs are inframarginal, there is no impact on auction outcomes, but provides 
significant assurances for the resource owner. If the resource is extramarginal as a result of these 
costs, the large load will bear the responsibility to replace it or be subject to IRAS service. 
50 The alternative may be generator bankruptcy that will benefit neither PJM, its 
customers nor the generator.

16 
should be permitted to bid economically into the BRA. PJM’s own filing acknowledges that a 
physical resource may support multiple BYONC arrangements, each of which may be in an 
arrangement with different New Large Loads.51 PJM provides no justification for requiring non-
BYONC MW to offer at zero when those MW are not committed to any New Large Load and 
would otherwise compete in the market on economic terms. To the extent PJM disagrees with 
this clarification, NRG requests that the Commission direct non-BYONC MW from the same 
Capacity Resource be permitted to offer economically into the RPM Auction. 
   
V. 
NRG SEEKS CLARIFICATION, OR IN THE ALTERNATIVE, TARIFF 
MODIFICATIONS, PERMITTING EXPANDED DEMAND RESPONSE 
CAPACITY TO BE TREATED AS NEW CAPACITY 
NRG has identified four areas in the IRAS Filing that lack clarity, and to the extent these 
areas are inconsistent with NRG’s requested clarification, are unjust and unreasonable because 
they are discriminatory. First, existing Demand Resources should be permitted to offer BYONC 
in excess of prior capacity offers as “new” capacity. Second, any resource that would qualify as 
“new” capacity can also be eligible to serve as replacement capacity for Demand Resources. 
Third, curtailment-based Demand Resources should be eligible for BYONC without requiring 
generation or storage assets at the location. Fourth, the methodology used to determine eligibility 
of Demand Resources must be defined. 
 
51 See Proposed Tariff, Attach. DD-4, section VII(f).

17 
First, NRG seeks clarification, or an amendment of the proposed tariff, that an existing 
Demand Resource could offer BYONC in excess of prior capacity offers,52 consistent with other 
Capacity Resources that may include uprates and Surplus Interconnection Service capacity.53 
With this clarification, additional investments may be encouraged at an existing “registered 
location” such as construction of behind-the-meter generation, on-site battery storage, or other 
customer-site enhancements, even if that resource previously supported a capacity 
commitment.54 Similarly, treating increased Demand Resource capacity as “new” capacity 
provides a comparable benefit to PJM customers.55 Thus, this clarification would ensure that 
Demand Resources are treated the same as other Capacity Resources and ensure that Demand 
Resources are available to offset New Large Loads.  
Second, the IRAS Filing does not clearly define what may serve as replacement capacity 
for BYONC Demand Resources, except that it would “need to be supported by the certification 
required by Tariff, Attachment DD-4, section VII(a)(ii)”, that circularly requires compliance with 
Attachment DD-4, Section VIII.56 NRG seeks clarification, or an amendment to the tariff, that 
any resource that would qualify as “new” capacity can also be eligible to serve as replacement

by the Commission.

Third, NRG seeks clarification that Demand Resources achieving load reductions through 
curtailment alone, without the installation of new generation or storage assets, are eligible for 
BYONC. As proposed, the IRAS tariff requires that demand-side BYONC be composed of 
locations “at which an incremental amount at that location is the result of the registration of new 
generation or storage assets at the location.”57 This language appears to compound the historical-
participation exclusion with a separate requirement for new physical assets at the location. If so, 
this would exclude the vast majority of curtailment-based Demand Resources, which achieve 
reductions through operational adjustments rather than new “generation or storage assets.” 
Curtailment-based Demand Resources provide the same reliability value as a generator obtaining 
new Capacity Interconnection Rights. Their exclusion would be unjust and discriminatory. 
Fourth, the methodology used to determine eligibility of Demand Resources must be 
defined. NRG recognizes that the demand-side BYONC replacement mechanism was developed 
through the CIFP stakeholder process and supports the concept of permitting replacement 
capacity for demand-side BYONC. However, the Commission must require PJM to provide 
clarity on how a Curtailment Service Provider (“CSP”) will be required to demonstrate each year 
of a 10-year period for a Demand Resource.58 Matters that significantly affect the rates, terms 
and conditions of service must be specified in the tariff.59 PJM’s proposed tariff states:

NRG seeks clarification that the 10-year demonstration is made by showing the “installed 
capacity for the first Delivery Year after the BYONC is in an arrangement with the New Large 
Load.”61 More specifically, that PJM’s proposed language does not mean that incremental 
customers that make up an aggregation must have a 10-year commitment to make this 
demonstration. If PJM disagrees with this interpretation, that would be unjust and unreasonable 
and unduly discriminatory, and NRG requests the Commission direct amendments.  
It must be recognized that a Demand Resource is typically an aggregated portfolio that 
may be composed of many Demand Resource registrations, each representing an individual 
customer location. Such aggregations are composed of heterogeneous and highly variable 
customers, each having different negotiated contract length and expirations and each of them 
experiencing changes in the way they consume electricity over time. Aggregation activities by 
CSPs are what allows a diverse, evolving group of customers to provide a firm capacity resource.

understood in any contractual arrangement as to render recitation superfluous.”).

In PJM, the quantum of Demand Resources that a customer can provide is capped at its 
Peak Load Contribution (“PLC”).62 Individual contributions to an aggregator’s portfolio change 
annually and may be difficult to predict more than one year into the future. Individual customer 
volumes of participating demand response expands and contracts based upon PLC as well as 
customer usage patterns. Businesses and homes change owners/tenants and new occupants may 
decide to start or stop participation in demand response. Technology evolves. Equipment gets old 
and may be replaced. Batteries, distributed generation, electric vehicles, etc., all can change 
customer PLC and load reduction capabilities. This diversity and the ebb and flow of customer 
demand response capabilities is managed by aggregators – who can add new customers to 
replace customers who depart or whose flexible capability declines. However, in the aggregate, 
the volume of the Demand Resource is reliable. 
PJM’s proposal, if interpreted inconsistently with NRG’s approach, would mandate 
individual customer locations to make the required eligibility showing for the full 10-year period. 
This is anathema to long-standing Commission-approved approaches for demand response 
portfolio management.63 The Commission should specify that Demand Resources may

CONCLUSION
